sentence: lactose malabsorption
note: NIDDK names lactose malabsorption as the underlying cause (loose alias).

sentence: Digestive symptoms such as bloating, diarrhoea and gas that follow eating or drinking foods that contain lactose, the sugar in milk.
note: NIDDK: digestive trouble such as bloating, diarrhea and gas after eating or drinking lactose-containing foods. "Sugar in milk" is a plain textbook fact.

sentence: Lactose intolerance means having digestive symptoms after eating or drinking foods that contain lactose.
It is linked to the small intestine not making enough lactase, the enzyme that digests lactose.
note: MedlinePlus: develops when the small intestine does not make enough of the enzyme; NHS lists too little lactase.

sentence: The NHS says it can start at any age.
note: NHS summary: can start at any age.

sentence: It is a different condition from a milk allergy.
note: NIDDK: different condition from milk allergy.

sentence: The NHS also says most adults with lactose intolerance do not need a severely restricted or lactose-free diet.
Not producing enough lactase, the enzyme that digests lactose
Bowel conditions, infections or injuries affecting the gut
note: NHS: bowel conditions, infections or injuries; NIDDK: injury to the small intestine (secondary lactose intolerance).

sentence: Lactase production falling after infancy (lactase nonpersistence), which can cause lactose intolerance in adulthood
Another health condition, such as coeliac disease, in some people
note: NHS 111 Wales: in some people caused by another condition such as coeliac disease.

sentence: Being born too early (premature birth)
note: MedlinePlus Genetics: babies born too early sometimes have lactose intolerance.

sentence: Family and genetic background, with lactase nonpersistence more common in some groups, including people of East Asian descent
note: MedlinePlus Genetics: most prevalent in East Asian descent; NIDDK: genes can be the reason in some cases.

sentence: A recent diarrhoeal illness, which can trigger temporary lactose intolerance
note: MedlinePlus: temporary diarrhoeal illness can trigger it.

sentence: Symptoms that follow foods containing lactose, found by asking about symptoms and eating habits
note: NIDDK: doctor asks about symptoms, family and medical history, eating habits.

sentence: Symptoms that improve when lactose is removed from the diet and return when it is put back
note: Elimination and reintroduction approach in NHS search results.

sentence: Lower calcium and vitamin D intake if all milk and dairy are cut out
note: NIDDK: cutting out all milk and dairy can reduce calcium and vitamin D intake.

sentence: Confusion with other conditions such as irritable bowel syndrome, which can cause similar symptoms
note: MedlinePlus: IBS can produce similar symptoms.

sentence: A doctor usually asks about symptoms, family and medical history and eating habits, and may examine the person and arrange tests to confirm lactose intolerance or rule out other problems.
The NHS says a GP may suggest a lactose elimination diet or a hydrogen breath test.
MedlinePlus describes breath, blood and stool tests, with the hydrogen breath test the most commonly used.
note: MedlinePlus: blood, breath or stool test; lactose-hydrogen breath test most common.

sentence: Most people can manage symptoms by eating less lactose or avoiding it.
Taking a lactase supplement before food or drink that contains lactose may reduce or prevent symptoms for some people.
The British Dietetic Association advises replacing dairy with lactose-free milk products or fortified plant-based alternatives.
note: BDA food intolerance fact sheet summary.

sentence: NIDDK recommends talking with a doctor or dietitian about dietary changes.
MedlinePlus says there is no known way to prevent lactose intolerance, although symptoms can be avoided by avoiding foods that contain lactose.
A routine GP appointment is the usual route if symptoms keep coming back, particularly after eating, or if there is persistent bloating, blood in the stool or unexplained weight loss.
note: NHS: see a GP if symptoms keep recurring; bloating, blood in stool, unexplained weight loss.

sentence: Anyone who thinks a child is lactose intolerant is advised by the NHS to see a GP before removing dairy from the diet.
The NHS says to call 999 for sudden confusion, dizziness, fainting or a limp, unresponsive child.
note: NHS emergency list (as returned; context of the full list not shown).

sentence: Lactose is the sugar found in milk and dairy foods.
Lactose intolerance means digestive trouble, such as bloating, diarrhoea and gas, after eating or drinking foods that contain it.
The underlying problem is lactose malabsorption, where the small intestine produces too little lactase, the enzyme that breaks lactose down.
note: NIDDK: lactose malabsorption, small intestine produces little lactase.

sentence: The NHS says lactose intolerance can start at any age.
It is a different condition from a milk allergy.
Tolerance varies, and NIDDK says research suggests many people can handle some lactose with no or only mild symptoms.
note: NIDDK: many people can handle about 12 g lactose with no or mild symptoms (figure deliberately omitted).

sentence: Lactose also appears in some packaged and prepared foods, and NIDDK says a small amount may be found in some prescription and over-the-counter medicines.
MedlinePlus says eating less food with lactose, or using pills or drops that help digest lactose, usually helps.
Common symptoms listed by the NHS include stomach pain or discomfort, bloating, gas, rumbling in the stomach, diarrhoea or constipation, and nausea or vomiting.
NIDDK says symptoms typically start within a few hours of eating lactose.
MedlinePlus says they usually appear roughly half an hour to two hours after dairy, and tend to be worse with larger amounts.
Because these symptoms are digestive and fairly general, other conditions can cause similar problems.
note: Textbook-level inference from MLP that IBS gives similar symptoms.

sentence: MedlinePlus notes that irritable bowel syndrome can produce similar symptoms.
A review of the evidence also notes that self-reported intolerance often does not match test results, so symptoms alone can mislead.
note: PMC review summary: self-reported intolerance unreliable diagnostic tool (blended summary; page not individually confirmed).

sentence: The NHS advises seeing a GP if symptoms keep coming back, especially after eating.
The NHS says causes include not producing enough lactase, and bowel conditions, infections or injuries.
In adults it can result from lactase nonpersistence, meaning lactase production is reduced after infancy.
NIDDK says genes can be the reason in some cases, and that injury to the small intestine can also cause it, which is called secondary lactose intolerance.
Babies born too early sometimes have lactose intolerance, according to MedlinePlus Genetics.
MedlinePlus says it is more common among adults of Asian, African or Native American heritage.
In some people another health condition, such as coeliac disease, is the cause, according to NHS 111 Wales.
Secondary intolerance, often following a gut infection, is mainly temporary, according to an NHS clinical guidance page.
note: Title carries secondary lactose intolerance; summary says mainly temporary after gastroenteritis.

sentence: MedlinePlus says that when a short diarrhoeal illness was the trigger, lactase levels typically recover within a few weeks.
A doctor usually asks about symptoms, family and medical history and eating habits.
The doctor may also carry out a physical examination and tests to confirm lactose intolerance or to rule out other problems.
The NHS says a GP may suggest a lactose elimination diet, in which lactose is removed from the diet and then put back to see whether symptoms return.
note: NHS search results describe removal then reintroduction.

sentence: The other approach the NHS describes is a hydrogen breath test, which measures hydrogen in the breath to see how well lactose is digested.
MedlinePlus says the lactose-hydrogen breath test is the most commonly used test.
It also describes a lactose tolerance blood test, which looks for a rise in blood glucose after a lactose drink.
MedlinePlus adds that a doctor may use a blood, breath or stool test to find out whether problems are due to lactose intolerance.
Most people can manage symptoms by eating less lactose or avoiding it, according to the NHS.
The NHS also says most adults with lactose intolerance do not need a severely restricted or lactose-free diet.
Taking a lactase supplement before food or drink that contains lactose may reduce or prevent symptoms for some people.
The British Dietetic Association advises replacing dairy with lactose-free milk products or fortified plant-based alternatives.
NIDDK says managing symptoms usually means adjusting intake rather than cutting out dairy entirely.
It warns that cutting out all milk and dairy can reduce calcium and vitamin D intake, and recommends talking with a doctor or dietitian about changes.
MedlinePlus says milk is a major source of calcium, so a person who does not get enough from the diet may need a calcium supplement.
MedlinePlus adds that symptoms can be avoided by avoiding foods that contain lactose, and that there is no known way to prevent the condition itself.
No, NIDDK describes lactose intolerance as a different condition from a milk allergy.
Lactose intolerance is linked to the small intestine making too little lactase, and it causes digestive symptoms such as bloating, diarrhoea and gas.
Anyone unsure which applies is advised by the NHS to see a GP if symptoms keep coming back.
Not necessarily, as the NHS says most adults with lactose intolerance do not need a severely restricted or lactose-free diet.
NIDDK says many people do not need to avoid all foods that contain lactose, and that cutting out all milk and dairy can reduce calcium and vitamin D intake.
A doctor or dietitian can advise on changes.
It depends on the cause.
note: Framing sentence summarising MedlinePlus and NHS guidance below.

sentence: When it follows a short diarrhoeal illness, MedlinePlus says lactase levels typically recover within a few weeks.
NHS clinical guidance describes secondary intolerance, often after a gut infection, as mainly temporary.
Where lactase production falls after infancy, MedlinePlus Genetics describes it as a reduction in lactase production.
The NHS says a GP may suggest a lactose elimination diet or a hydrogen breath test.
The breath test measures hydrogen in the breath to see how well lactose is digested.
MedlinePlus also describes a lactose tolerance blood test, which looks for a rise in blood glucose after a lactose drink, and says stool tests may be used.
The NHS says taking a lactase supplement before having food or drink that contains lactose may reduce or prevent symptoms for some people.
MedlinePlus says pills or drops that help digest lactose usually help, together with eating less lactose.
A doctor or dietitian can advise on whether they suit a particular person.
note: NIDDK recommends talking to doctor or dietitian about dietary changes.
